summary: Describes a minimal mode of operation for IPv6 over the TSCH mode of IEEE 802.15.4e networks. It names the baseline protocols, configurations and modes needed for a functioning 6TiSCH network. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Tiny devices hop between radio channels at set times. This lists the basic settings so they can all talk to each other.

questions: how does a node join a 6tisch network
what is an enhanced beacon in tsch
subtitle: The baseline settings every 6TiSCH device needs so tiny, channel-hopping radios can form an IPv6 network and talk to each other.

tldr.problem: IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH links has many knobs, and devices from different makers cannot interoperate unless they start from the same settings.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes a minimal mode: one slotframe with a single shared cell for beacons and data, default timeslot and hopping settings, RPL with Objective Function 0, and rules for how nodes join and keep time.
tldr.outcome: Every 6TiSCH-compliant device should implement this minimal mode. It gives enough bandwidth to bootstrap the network and its security, and leaves dynamic scheduling to future work.

today: RFC 8180 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 210) published in May 2017. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The text expects future specifications to add dynamic schedule management on top of this minimal mode.

sections.title: Why a Minimal Mode
sections.content:
A 6TiSCH network carries IPv6 (RFC 2460) over a Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) mesh made of IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH links. The pieces used are the 6LoWPAN framework (RFC 4944, RFC 6282, RFC 8025, RFC 8138, RFC 6775), RPL (RFC 6550) and RPL Objective Function 0 (RFC 6552). All of them are used unmodified.

This RFC adds the operating parameters and procedures that make nodes interoperate. Nodes learn a communication schedule when they join, and under this specification that schedule is the same for all nodes and never changes. Dynamic scheduling is explicitly out of scope and expected from future work.

The minimal configuration provides the bandwidth nodes need to bootstrap the network, including initial configuration and security bootstrapping. An implementation MUST support IEEE 802.15.4 in TSCH mode. If this RFC and the IEEE standard disagree, the IEEE standard wins.
sections.eli5: Many small gadgets need to agree on one basic way of talking before they can do fancy things. This document is that basic agreement.

sections.title: The Single-Slotframe Schedule
sections.content:
The minimal mode uses a single slotframe, a repeating set of timeslots. Its size is tunable and trades bandwidth against energy; how to tune it is out of scope, and the size is announced in the beacons. The recommended slotframe handle is 0x00.

Only one cell in the slotframe is scheduled. It may sit at any slot offset and channel offset, and its location is announced in the beacon. Its link type is ADVERTISING so that beacons can be sent on it. All other cells are left unscheduled for future dynamic scheduling, for example the 6top Protocol (6P).

In that one cell a node transmits if it has a packet and listens otherwise, so both the TX and RX bits are set. The Shared bit is set so that a node that sends and gets no acknowledgment backs off to resolve collisions. The Timekeeping bit is set so a joining node can stay synchronized to its initial time-source neighbor. Beacons go to the link-layer broadcast address and are not acknowledged. Data frames are unicast and acknowledged.

The default IEEE timeslot template (macTimeslotTemplateId=0) and default channel hopping sequence (macHoppingSequenceID = 0) SHOULD be used. The recommended maximum is 3 retransmissions, so 4 attempts in total, after which the link layer MUST tell the upper layer the transmission failed. Frames that need no acknowledgment, including beacons, are not retransmitted.
sections.eli5: There is one special meeting slot that repeats again and again. Everyone either talks or listens in it, and politely waits and retries if two kids talk at once.

sections.title: Frame Contents and Enhanced Beacons
sections.content:
The Frame Version field MUST be set to 0b10 (Frame Version 2), and the Sequence Number field MAY be elided. A beacon's destination address MUST be 0xFFFF, the short broadcast address. Its source address SHOULD be the node's short address if supported, otherwise the long address MUST be used.

A node that boots is unsynchronized and unjoined, and it syncs by listening for Enhanced Beacons (EBs). IEEE 802.15.4 does not say how often EBs are sent, so the RFC says a node SHOULD send one every EB_PERIOD. A shorter period joins faster but costs more energy. EBs SHOULD carry four Information Elements: TSCH Synchronization (including the ASN and Join Metric), TSCH Timeslot, Channel Hopping, and TSCH Slotframe and Link.

If a node follows the recommended settings exactly, the EB it sends is identical to the one it received, except for the Join Metric. A node that has already joined SHOULD ignore later EBs that try to change its configured parameters. Each acknowledgment carries an ACK/NACK Time Correction IE.
sections.eli5: Beacons are like a lighthouse flashing the time and the timetable. A new device watches them to learn when to talk and which channel to use.

sections.title: Link-Layer Security and Keys
sections.content:
Any link-layer security MUST use the mechanisms in IEEE 802.15.4. Authentication MUST cover the entire frame including the header, while encryption MAY be applied to payload IEs and the payload. The RFC assumes two keys: K1 authenticates EBs, which MUST be authenticated only and not encrypted, and K2 authenticates and encrypts data and acknowledgment frames.

What a joining node does depends on which keys it already has:

  • Both K1 and K2 pre-configured: no key distribution is needed.
  • Only K1 pre-configured: it authenticates EBs with K1 and learns K2 during key distribution.
  • Neither: it accepts EBs as IEEE 802.15.4 allows even if unsecuring reported an error, then runs key distribution to learn K1 and K2. The node helping it uses the secExempt mechanism and MUST clear those exception rules afterward.

After a network reset, the new network MUST either use new keys or ensure the ASN keeps increasing monotonically. Key distribution mechanisms are out of scope.
sections.eli5: There are two secret passwords. One proves the lighthouse signals are real, and the other keeps normal messages private.

sections.title: RPL Settings
sections.content:
In a multi-hop topology RPL MAY be used. If it is, nodes MUST implement Objective Function Zero (OF0). A node's rank is R(N) = R(P) + rank_increment, where rank_increment = (Rf*Sp + Sr) * MinHopRankIncrease. The values that MUST be used are Rf = 1, Sr = 0, MinHopRankIncrease = 256, and Sp = (3*ETX)-2, based on the Expected Transmission Count. Candidate parents with an ETX greater than 3 SHOULD NOT be selected.

Nodes MUST implement RPL non-storing mode, and nodes with enough capability SHOULD also implement storing mode. Nodes that do not implement RPL MUST join as leaf nodes. DIOs use the Trickle timer with the RPL default values. RPL headers MUST follow RFC 6553 and RFC 6554 and be compressed per RFC 8138 and RFC 8025.
sections.eli5: Each device picks a neighbor closer to the boss to pass messages through, and it chooses neighbors whose messages usually get through the first time.

sections.title: Network Formation and Lifetime
sections.content:
The Join Metric in the TSCH Synchronization IE MUST be calculated from the node's routing metric, normalized to a value between 0 and 255. Lower means closer to the root and more preferred. With RPL it MUST be DAGRank(rank)-1, which gives the root a Join Metric of 0.

Which neighbor to sync to first is implementation specific. A node MAY wait at most MAX_EB_DELAY seconds for EBs from NUM_NEIGHBOURS_TO_WAIT distinct neighbors and pick using the Join Metric. At all times a node MUST stay synchronized to at least one time-source neighbor, chosen from its RPL parent set when RPL is used. If it loses all of them it must join again.

A RPL node MUST NOT send EBs until it has acquired a RPL rank, and SHOULD start once it has. To stop constant parent flapping, the RFC recommends a PARENT_SWITCH_THRESHOLD of 640 for the ((3*ETX)-2)*minHopRankIncrease metric. This covers both routing parent and time-source neighbor selection.
sections.eli5: New devices listen for the neighbor closest to the boss. Nobody starts flashing signals until they know their own place in the line, and nobody switches friends over a tiny difference.

sections.title: Implementation Recommendations
sections.content:
The neighbor table format is implementation specific, but the RFC recommends keeping per neighbor an identifier, numTx, numTxAck, numRx, a timestamp of the last frame, a routing metric and a time-source flag. The RFC takes this list from the openwsn implementation.

For queues, a node keeps a configurable number of upper-layer packets per link (NUM_UPPERLAYER_PACKETS) for a configurable time covering the join process (MAX_JOIN_TIME). Frames generated by the 802.15.4 layer, including EBs, are queued ahead of frames from higher layers, and BEACON frames ahead of DATA frames. The recommended values are 180 for MAX_EB_DELAY, 2 for NUM_NEIGHBOURS_TO_WAIT, 640 for PARENT_SWITCH_THRESHOLD, 1 for NUM_UPPERLAYER_PACKETS and 300 for MAX_JOIN_TIME.
sections.eli5: Each device keeps a small notebook about its neighbors and lets the important signals go to the front of the line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC covers only link-layer security. It assumes nodes in exposed places will be compromised and their keys extracted, so fixed secrets will not stay secret and provisioning a fixed link key K2 is not secure. For most applications there will be a joining phase in which some unauthenticated nodes are allowed.

If an attacker has K1 it can send authenticated fake EBs. If neither key is pre-provisioned, a joiner may mistake a fake EB for a real one and start joining the attacker. That join fails, but costs the node time and energy. Radio jamming is the base case for denial of service. A fake EB announcing a very low Join Metric can also waste a node's effort.

Any reuse of an ASN with a key exposes information about encrypted contents and risks replay, which is why a reset network needs new keys or a monotonic ASN. The 6TiSCH layer SHOULD track anomalies, such as integrity-check failures on packets with a valid CRC, which should occur on the order of once per million packets, and time updates inconsistent with plausible clock drift.
sections.eli5: Bad actors can flash fake lighthouse signals to waste a newcomer's time, so devices should watch for odd behavior and keep their secret passwords safe.
